summary: Remove duplicates in place from a sorted array and return the number of unique elements.
mainInsight: In a sorted array duplicates are adjacent, so keep a write pointer j for the last unique element and copy any element different from nums[j] to j + 1.

approaches.name: Set + rebuild
approaches.summary: Collect unique values and write them back.

approaches.name: Read/write pointers
approaches.summary: i scans; when nums[i] != nums[j], write it at j + 1.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. Starting i at 1 would skip the self-comparison.

promptVariants: Which technique solves this problem, and what in the statement or constraints points to it?
Name the technique you would use here and the clue in the problem that tells you.
What approach fits this problem, and which part of the statement gives it away?
cards.answer: Read and write pointers: copy an element forward when it differs from the last unique value. Clue: The array is sorted so duplicates are adjacent, and it must be edited in place, so keep a write pointer for the next unique value.
keyPoints: The array is sorted so duplicates are adjacent, and it must be edited in place, so keep a write pointer for the next unique value.
cards.explanation: Sorted order puts equal values together, so comparing each element with the last kept one is enough.

rubric.technique: Read and write pointers: copy an element forward when it differs from the last unique value

alsoValid.name: Collect the unique values in a set and write them back
alsoValid.note: correct, but uses extra space and ignores the sorted order

promptVariants: Which pattern performs in-place deduplication of a sorted array?
What technique uses one pointer to read and another to write?
cards.explanation: The write index trails the read index and only advances on new values. (Read/write two pointers: fast/slow)

incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash set: Not needed because duplicates are adjacent (and sets use extra space).

promptVariants: What is true about nums[0..j] at every step?
State the invariant for the write pointer j.
cards.answer: nums[0..j] holds the distinct values seen so far in sorted order, and nums[j] is the most recent unique value (the one to compare against).

promptVariants: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place takes ___ time.
The read/write-pointer deduplication uses ___ extra space.
cards.explanation: Two indices; modifications are in place.

promptVariants: Why compare against nums[j] rather than nums[i - 1], and why is the return j + 1?
What does j represent when the loop ends?
cards.answer: nums[j] is the last unique value already placed; a different nums[i] is new. Comparing with nums[i - 1] also works for sorted input, but nums[j] is the more direct invariant. j is the index of the last unique element, so the count is j + 1.
keyPoints: Compare with last written unique value

options: 1 (the loop never advances j, so it returns j + 1)

cards.answer: 1 (the loop never advances j, so it returns j + 1)
cards.explanation: With one element nothing is written and the count is 1.
